passages.original: XIX. Ut Constans Imperator, pro Athanasio, fratri Constantio scripserit, eumque Ec- clesiae suae reddi jusserit.
passages.english: XIX. How the emperor Constans wrote to his brother Constantius on behalf of Athanasius, and ordered that he be restored to his church.

passages.original: Huic accidit presbyterum quendam venire in notitiam, latenter partibus Arii faventem. Sed is primo nihil omnino de his apud sororem Principis aperire : ubi vero multa familia- ritas copiam tribuit, paulatim sermonem coepit aspergere [Al. aperire], invidiam dicens Ario ge- neratam, et pro simultatibus privatis Episcopum suum rem contentiose exagitavisse, aemulationis sti- mulo confixum, quod Arius apud plebem satis carus haleretur. Haec atque hujusmodi alia frequentius suggerens, animos Constantiae suos a efficit.
passages.english: It happened that a certain presbyter came to her notice who secretly favoured the party of Arius. At first he disclosed nothing at all about these matters to the emperor's sister; but when great intimacy gave him the opportunity, he gradually began to sprinkle his talk [with them], saying that ill will had been stirred up against Arius, and that his bishop had contentiously stirred the matter up out of private grudges, pierced by the goad of jealousy, because Arius was held very dear by the people. By suggesting these and other things of this kind quite often, he made Constantia's mind his own.
passages.notes: "suos a efficit": the stray "a" is taken as a footnote mark; "animos ... suos efficit" is understood as "won her over to his side". A variant reading has "aperire" ("to disclose") for "aspergere" ("to sprinkle").

passages.original: Arium ne- quicquam apud Alexandriam commorantem venire a facit, et Imperialibus edictis concilium dentio Con- stantinopolum convocari. Quo convenere illi maxime, qui Arium atque Eusebium sectabantur, quique saepe cum Alexandro congressi, ut Arium suscipe- ret, nec tamen aliquid b profligantes, ab injuriis quidem ejus temperabant. Ad (??)imum certam c ei diem statuentes denuntiant, ni aut ipse Arium sus- ciperet, aut si reniteretur, se Ecclesta pulso et in exilium truso, ab alio eum suscipiendum sciret.
passages.english: He had Arius, who was staying at Alexandria to no purpose, come [to court], and by imperial edicts had a council convoked again at Constantinople. Those who gathered there were chiefly the ones who followed Arius and Eusebius. They had often met with Alexander [to press him] to receive Arius, and though they achieved nothing, they did at least refrain from wronging him. At last they fixed a set day for him and gave him notice: either he himself would receive Arius, or, if he resisted, he should know that he would be driven from the Church and thrust into exile, and Arius would be received by someone else.
passages.notes: "dentio" read as "denuo" (again). "Ad (??)imum" read as "ad ultimum" (at last). Stray letters a, b, c are taken as footnote marks. "Ecclesta" read as "Ecclesia" throughout.

passages.original: Quod postea quam in Ecclesta nuntiatum est Eusebio, atque his qui una secum sanctum et innocentem virum Alexan- drum de Ario recipiendo fatigabant, superati pudore, et adoperti confusione discedunt. Tunc completus est sermo ad gloriam Domini, quem Alexander in oratione sua ad Deum [Al Dominum] proclamave- rat, dicens : Judica, Domine, inter me et Eusebii minas atque Arii g vim. Sed haec ad praesens quidem paululum pudor(??)s habuere. Convenientes vero inter se haeretici, veriti ne forte si, sicut res gesta est, integre ad Imperatorem Constantium pervenisset, non solum a perfidia cotum, h in qua callide irreti- tus tenebatur, abscederet : verum et in auctores de- ceptionis suae seveiius aliquid ex regia auctoritate decerneret, componunt [Al. ponunt] per eunuchos quos jam 1 perlidia d(??)cep(??)s tenebant, uti de Arii morte Imperator quam fieri posset composite et communiter nosceret, neque aliquid quod Dei vin- dictam indicare viderelur, audiret. Quibus ita gestis, de caussa fidei ut coeperant, prosequuntur.
passages.english: After this was announced in the church to Eusebius and to those who, together with him, had been wearying the holy and innocent man Alexander about receiving Arius, they went away overcome with shame and covered with confusion. Then the word that Alexander had cried out in his prayer to God was fulfilled, to the glory of the Lord, when he said: "Judge, Lord, between me and the threats of Eusebius and the violence of Arius." But for the present this brought them a little shame. The heretics, however, met together, fearing that if the matter reached the Emperor Constantius whole, just as it had happened, he might not only withdraw from their faithlessness, in which he was cunningly entangled, but might also decree something rather severe by royal authority against the authors of his deception. So they arranged, through the eunuchs whom they already held deceived by their faithlessness, that the emperor should learn of Arius' death in as composed and ordinary a form as possible, and should hear nothing that might seem to point to God's vengeance. When this had been done, they pursued the cause of the faith as they had begun.
passages.notes: "cotum" read as "eorum" (their). "perlidia d(??)cep(??)s" read as "perfidia deceptos". The text names the emperor as Constantius; the narrative context suggests Constantine, so this may be an error in the text. "pudor(??)s habuere" read as "pudoris habuere". Variant readings: "Dominum" for "Deum"; "ponunt" for "componunt".

passages.original: Prima introducitur accusatio mulie- ris cujusdam, quae se diceret aliquando hospitio Athanasium recepisse [Al. suscepisse], et ab eo no- ctu nihil suspicantem, vim corruptionis esse perpes- sam. Introduci ad haec jubetur Athanasius : ingredi- tur cum Timotheo presbytero siu, eumque monet, ut posteaquam mulier dicendi finem fecisset, se ta- cente, e ipse ad ea quae dixerat responderet. Cum- que mulier ea quae edocta fuerat, perorasset, Timo- theus conversus 245 ad eam : Vere, inquit, mulier, ego mansi apud te aliquando, aut vim tibi, ut asse- ris, feci?
passages.english: First the accusation of a certain woman is brought in, who claimed that she had once received Athanasius as a guest, and that during the night, while she suspected nothing, she had suffered violent defilement at his hands. Athanasius is ordered to be brought in to answer this. He enters with his presbyter Timothy, and instructs him that, after the woman had finished speaking, he himself should reply to what she had said while Athanasius kept silent. And when the woman had finished the speech she had been taught, Timothy turned to her and said: "Woman, did I really stay with you once, or did I do violence to you, as you claim?"
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'siu' read as 'suo', and a stray 'e' before 'ipse' omitted. The number '245' in the text is a page marker and has been left out. The edition gives 'suscepisse' as an alternative reading for 'recepisse' ('received'); the sense is the same.
